This is spot on. It would be a shame if we get AGI for enterprise productivity and miss on AGI for scientific acceleration. Can't let it happen.
Quoting @fidjissimo
I disagree with Dario on most things, but this is spot on: “At this point, saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliché than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive. The thing that will work is actually curing cancer.”
The thing that frustrates me is that some people often draw a straight line from smarter models → cures, without acknowledging how much infrastructure is missing in between. We’ve still got a lot of work to do, people.
The regulatory bottleneck gets a lot of attention. But the bigger bottleneck may be that in many places, we’re lacking the right biological data. AI can’t reason its way to cures if we haven’t generated the data required to understand the disease in the first place.
Ironically, that’s why I’m most bullish on AI making dramatic progress in cancer first: decades of investment have produced extraordinary datasets across genomics, pathology, imaging, clinical outcomes, and more.
For complex chronic diseases, much of that infrastructure simply doesn’t exist yet. The good news is that many companies (including @ChronicleBioAI) are racing to build it.
But model intelligence and biological infrastructure are going to have to scale together. I really do believe AI can cure all diseases but only if we build the infrastructure to translate intelligence into cures at the same pace that models improve (which is a high bar!). Otherwise, we risk having superintelligent AI with an incomplete picture of human biology, and delay that promise by years.

I was the first White House Special Advisor for AI. My friend Tantum Collins was Director for Technology and National Security, joining government after five years at Google DeepMind. Today, I’m a professor at Johns Hopkins and an advisor to Anthropic and others, and Tantum is the CEO of Inherent.
Long before we served in government, we thought that humanity was on track to create AI systems that outperform humans at virtually every cognitive task. This was once a fringe hypothesis. It now seems inevitable.
THE BITTER STRUGGLE is our new book about what’s happened, what’s coming, and what’s at stake. From nanometer-scale chips to gigawatt data centers, we will show you why AI is so powerful, and why its progress will accelerate from here in ways that feel like science fiction. We will take you into the Oval Office with President Biden, the Situation Room with the Cabinet, and the Roosevelt Room with leading CEOs — and we will examine what has happened under President Trump. The decisions made in these rooms, and in Silicon Valley, will determine which nations gain a decisive lead in AI. Whoever wields that technology will gain a power unlike any in history. The next few years may decide the next few decades.
But, most of all, together we will confront AI’s hardest questions. What is the proper relationship between the companies inventing the technology, the government, and the public? How can we make sure AI is safe and trustworthy? How do democracies win without losing our values?
And how can humanity figure all of this out when we are so quickly running out of time?
That question is why we wrote this book — and why we believe the answers are too important to only be debated in closed rooms, including the ones we once sat in. We are so excited to finally share our work with you.

Folks in the AI and AI safety community have for years been puzzling over Sam's and OpenAI's position on questions related to AI safety. A narrative that took root in the safety community was that OpenAI didn't care enough about it, or didn't take it adequately seriously. This narrative has always struck me as wrong. I hope it will become increasingly clear to everyone that OpenAI does in fact care about safety and is going to do whatever is necessary to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity.
Sam, Greg, and other leaders at OpenAI have always been open to, and taken seriously, the possibility that sufficiently advanced AI would require extraordinary effort to manage risks. They have always been clear in their communications that they expected there was going to be a line at some point, beyond which there would need to be a different approach than was needed for consumer chat models. And they were also clear that it was contingent on the actual capabilities of the models.
They walked a fine line: they hosted, funded, and supported a huge amount of safety and alignment research and consistently messaged in favor of AI safety work. At the same time they also got consistently pummeled by this community. Despite getting constantly beaten up they didn't turn against it and they didn't punch back. They have maintained a principled and difficult position.
I expect in the long term people will look back on their leadership very favorably for this.

Model progress is now extremely rapid, and we always said we would take action if we felt that model capabilities were outstripping the pace of safety and alignment.
We care very deeply about AI safety. We believe the entire field will have to coordinate on shared safety standards, but will act unilaterally in the meantime.

An important first step in the drug development process is designing a molecule that can bind tightly to its target. We wanted to test if Claude could successfully design novel protein binders from scratch (also called de novo design). With a protein design prompt written by a human expert, Claude autonomously designed protein binders against 14 out of 15 targets.

title: Alex Imas (@alexolegimas)
clean_title: Behavioral economics highlights the limits of pure rationality and intelligence in predicting human care and decision-making
summary:
I taught behavioral economics for almost 15 years, first at Carnegie Mellon then UChicago. Every year I’d start the class with this example to illustrate how pure rationality fails in terms of predicting what people actually care about, particularly when it comes to social situations. We spent the rest of the class building a framework that would capture this.
It also illustrates the limits of trusting pure intelligence to get to outcomes we as humans care about. Von Neumann was one of the smartest people to ever walk the earth, but he had little understanding of what made people fulfilled or what they would be extremely upset by. He needed to be guided and sometimes overruled by “regular people”.
Quoting @geoffreyirving
One of the most inspiring thoughts I've heard in the last year was from a former Secretary of the Navy, when I asked him what he thought about game theoretic dynamics around the superintelligence ramp potentially driving us to kinetic war over the coming years.
They noted that historically during the Cold War, a range of people were advocating very strongly for nuclear first strikes. Some of these were coming from a military perspective (Curtis LeMay), but others such as von Neumann argued that game theory said first strike was optimal.
And then both these camps went (directly or indirectly) to various presidents, who said "No this is crazy, we're not going to kill millions of people based on your theoretical argument" (paraphrased).
I think this is an important heuristic to keep in mind when modeling the behaviors of actual humans, both because it has the potential to capture unmodeled aspects of the game theory and also because...sometimes people just refuse to do unreasonable things, even if the theory says they should.
Not all the ways in which we aren't modeled by game theory are good, but I think this is a hopeful thought on net, and it might be the thing that gets us through the next few years or decades intact.
clean_summary:
Alex Imas, with nearly 15 years of teaching behavioral economics, illustrates how pure rationality often fails to predict what people truly care about, especially in social contexts. This shows that even the most intelligent individuals, like von Neumann, lack understanding of human fulfillment and emotional responses, requiring guidance from ordinary people.

A quote from @geoffreyirving reflects on how game theory influenced Cold War nuclear strategies, with some leaders advocating first strikes based on theoretical models, only to be overruled by political leaders recognizing the unreasonableness of such actions. This suggests that humans often refuse to follow purely rational or theoretical predictions, which can be a hopeful sign for navigating complex future challenges.

title: Alex Imas (@alexolegimas)
summary:
Claude Science is an amazing tool. But, as @pdhsu has pointed out, these binders weren’t designed by Claude, but rather by domain-specific models, most of which are publicly available, like RFdiffusion.
Maybe this is a good time to explain the whole science behind this a bit, as well as the history of these models.
A “binder” in this case is simply a protein or a fragment of a protein engineered to stick tightly and selectively to another protein. One example is a molecule that can latch onto a receptor and prevent it from interacting with its normal partner, thus blocking its function. Optimising "binders" is just one small part of the drug discovery pipeline.
We already have AI models that are very good at the task of binder design. These models have been extensively trained on relevant domain specific data: int his case, protein structure data.
One example is RFdiffusion, a de novo protein design model which was published in 2023. Unlike AlphaFold, which predicts existing protein structure from sequence, RFDiffusion can generate new candidate protein structures, including structures shaped to bind a specified patch on another protein.
RFDiffusion was built by taking RoseTTAFold, a protein-structure-prediction model, (so similar in nature to AlphaFold, which was released in 2021, and retraining it as a diffusion model. What researchers did in practice was take experimentally determined protein structures from the Protein Data Bank, added noise to their coordinates, and taught the model to reconstruct them. The original RFdiffusion paper was already demonstrating experimentally validated binders with nanomolar affinities and a 19% hit rate on several test targets.
So the core of this technology was not created through Claude. The key models for protein design are now three to five years old. What Claude adds is still amazing useful and labour saving (I've written about how I'm excited about it before), but imo it acts more like a very useful interface and orchestrator.
Quoting @AnthropicAI
Many drugs work by binding to a specific target in the body and blocking or changing what it does. An important first step in the drug development process is designing a molecule that can bind tightly to its target. Traditionally, that's meant weeks or months of expert work per target, sifting through a large number of candidates to identify the few that work.
We wanted to test if Claude could successfully design novel protein binders from scratch (also called de novo design). With a protein design prompt written by a human expert, Claude autonomously designed protein binders against 14 out of 15 targets.
We then worked with Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience, who independently built and tested the proteins Claude designed.

title: Alex Imas (@alexolegimas)
clean_title: Current AI systems do not exhibit drives for power or self-preservation, contrary to some predictions
summary:
I don't think what Omohundro predicted is true with regards to current systems, ie these behaviours do not seem like drives for power, self preservation or anything of the sort. The behaviour of a reward hacking model is explained by poor RL practices/post training environments, not by an inmate drive of the model trying to shut anything down or seek power to reach its goal or escape.
One has to wonder why they occur in these complex cyber offense or extremely hard coding evals but not in everyday prosaic use; I think nostalgebraist demystifies this well here:
You can easily have other models not acting this way when given the same task (ie hacking is not a necessarily instrumentally convergent behavior - it just happens to be a path taken *given* a number of factors pushing the agent towards this direction).
There's a weak version of instrumental convergence that is pretty banal: yes models will do useful things if they help you reach a goal. If the path to the goal is underspecified, then it shouldn't too surprising that they aren't always taking the "optimal" path - especially if you RL then aggressively on evals with poor construct validity etc.
This is ultimately fixable though, not an immutable property of an "optimizer". I agree that today's AI labs aren't particularly good at specifying the relevant sub goals/pathways/processes to be integrated well with their RL; though I'm cautiously optimistic that this too will be ironed out, the incentives are there. That and, ultimately, better scaffolds/MAS and engineering practices generally.
The agents' propensity to help other AIs is also not really that novel, and likely a consequence of training models on multi agent traces. This of course comes with risks - see - but is not some emergent sinister property of better capabilities, or necessarily relating to a takeover scenario.
It also seems odd for some people to view this situation as "they're smart enough to solve Erdos problems and find hard CVEs, but dumb enough to actually attempt an escape and get caught." This really underestimates how capable the models are. Ultimately I think the ontology we use for goals, intelligence etc is wrong, at least with existing systems.
To be clear I'm not arguing these behaviours are fine or that they don't cause risks - but I think interpreting them as evidence of these earlier theories is a stretch. The early theories got certain things directionally right (eg applying principal agents to computational systems) and appreciated the importance of AI early, but also have a long list of incorrect views/beliefs too.
clean_summary: The prediction that AI systems develop drives for power or self-preservation is not supported by current behaviors. Reward hacking often results from poor RL practices and environment design, not from an inmate drive of the model. Such behaviors tend to appear in complex or hard evaluation scenarios but are less common in everyday use, especially when models are not pushed towards instrumentally convergent goals. Improving goal specification, RL practices, and engineering can mitigate these issues. Additionally, models' propensity to assist other AIs is likely due to training on multi-agent data, not emergent sinister properties. The idea that models are capable of solving complex problems but would attempt to escape is an underestimation of their capabilities. Overall, interpreting these behaviors as evidence of early theories about AI drives is a stretch, as current systems do not inherently possess such motivations.

title: Alex Imas (@alexolegimas)
clean_title: Alex Imas praises Daron Acemoglu's contributions and integrity amid critique
summary:
Agree with the below. I have never met @DAcemogluMIT nor interacted with him, but I’ve learned so much from his work.
Some of us still remember what political economy was like before Daron and his frequent collaborators Simon Johnson and James Robinson started writing papers: stable democracies, median voter theorem, public choice (with a few noteworthy exceptions). Introducing endogenous institutions, power, conflict, the role of commitment devices in governance, natural limits to authoritarianism, some of the central questions of our time, into economics, this was largely due to them.
Yes people disagree with Daron; I disagree with him on much as well. That’s all part of science.
The economist article is a good opportunity to take stock and recognize the contribution.
Quoting @erikbryn
.@TheEconomist is a great publication, and I’ve learned a lot from it over the years. But I think it missed the mark with this article on @DAcemogluMIT.
Daron and I publicly and privately disagree on a number of important issues, most notably on the likely magnitude of AI’s productivity effects in the coming years. We’ve had many lengthy discussions about our differences, including as recently as last month.
That said, Daron is not merely one of the most intelligent, interesting, and hardworking economists I know. He is also a person of great integrity.
Since many people may form their impressions of him from this article or other public commentary, let me offer three anecdotes from my own experience.
1. In 2017, @tommmitchell and I co-chaired a @theNASciences committee on information technology and the workforce, bringing together a dozen leading scholars. Committee members were unpaid, and there was little extrinsic reward for doing more than the minimum. Everyone contributed, but unquestionably the person who worked hardest, and produced the most high-quality substantive material, was Daron. I came away enormously impressed by his seriousness and work ethic.
2. The article suggests that Daron’s stature may discourage others from criticizing him. That has not been my experience. I remember an MIT seminar where he presented an early version of his work on robots and employment. He was subjected to exceptionally tough criticism from colleagues and graduate students, especially over his instrumental variables and other aspects of his empirical strategy. It was one of the toughest seminars I can remember. Nobody was pulling punches. If anything, the criticism was blunter because everyone knew Daron was perfectly capable of handling it.
3. Along with @professor_ajay, @akorinek, and @testingham, I helped lead the recent “We Must Act Now” statement on AI ( One of the first people we approached was Daron precisely because he had disagreed with me about AI capabilities and their likely economic effects. Daron and I went back and forth over the detailed wording for about a week. We ultimately found common ground. In the process, I was reminded of both his openness to new data and his attention to detail.
The Economist correctly highlights some important weaknesses in the economics profession. It should certainly scrutinize the work of prominent economists, presenting arguments and counterarguments.
In my view, what undermined their case was the article’s shift from criticizing his arguments to innuendo about Daron's personality. The suggestion that economists are unwilling to challenge him does not match what I have observed over 3 decades of knowing him.
Criticize Daron’s ideas and conclusions, as I often do. But the personal insinuations struck me as unfair.
clean_summary: Alex Imas agrees with the importance of Daron Acemoglu's work in integrating political economy into economics, highlighting his influence on topics like institutions, power, and conflict. Imas shares personal anecdotes demonstrating Acemoglu's dedication, work ethic, and openness to critique, countering the suggestion that his stature discourages criticism. He emphasizes that the recent Economist article unfairly shifted from critiquing ideas to making personal insinuations, which do not reflect his experience of Acemoglu's integrity and engagement over three decades.

clean_title: Personalized mRNA cancer vaccine passes Phase 3, promising for melanoma treatment
summary:
A personalized mRNA cancer vaccine passed Phase 3, genuinely great news for melanoma patients!
What happens here? They sequence your tumor, find up to 34 mutations unique to it, and build a custom vaccine that trains your immune system to hunt those exact cells.
In a phase 2 trial earlier this year the vaccine with immunotherapy has shown ~49% lower risk of recurrence or death vs immunotherapy alone, which is the current standard of care. We are waiting now for the details of the phase 3.
After that that concept is now expanding to lung, kidney, bladder cancer and hopefully to many more to come.
Huge win for science!
clean_summary: A personalized mRNA cancer vaccine has passed Phase 3 trials, marking a significant advance for melanoma patients. The vaccine is created by sequencing a patient's tumor, identifying up to 34 unique mutations, and building a custom vaccine to train the immune system to target those specific cells. In a Phase 2 trial earlier this year, the vaccine combined with immunotherapy reduced the risk of recurrence or death by approximately 49% compared to immunotherapy alone, which is the current standard of care. The results are encouraging, and the concept is now expanding to treat lung, kidney, and bladder cancers, with hopes for many more types in the future. This represents a major breakthrough for cancer immunotherapy.

In his 2014 book, Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies, he delved into various scenarios — like the now-famous “paperclip maximizer” — to show the dangers that unfettered and highly intelligent AI posed to humans. A decade later, in Deep Utopia: Life and Meaning in a Solved World, he looked at the other side of the AI coin, and theorizes what human experience might look like if AI is capable of solving all of our problems. What happens if AI and robots can literally do every single thing better than humans can? How would we find any meaning or satisfaction from life? title: Alex Imas (@alexolegimas)
summary:
I discuss the Moderna cancer vaccine results. They are exciting but we haven't cured cancer!
Some clarifications:
1. It doesn't clear cancer, it prevents recurrence after treatment.
2. We mostly "knew" because a phase 2b result was already posted 2 years ago. We don't actually know the effect size in this Phase 3, as the company hasn't disclosed. They're just saying it looks positive.
3. This is the cancer type where you'd expect this type of therapy to work the best. melanoma responds to all types of immunotherapy very well.
4. We already know similar vaccines from eg biontech failed in other solid cancers. It's gonna be a process of trial and error.
5. Cancer vaccines are not the most promising or potent type of cancer therapy, imo. It's CAR-Ts (which clear existing tumours) and now more recently in vivo CAR-Ts (enabled by mRNA technology, too).
Why are people so excited?

2. Moderna is a well known name.
3. mRNAs are controversial and make spirits rise in both directions.
Why has the stock risen so much?
1. It was a short squeeze.
2. Moderna is known to generalist investors, whereas many biotechs are not.
3. People expect Moderna's platform to generalise to other cancers.
4. Moderna was running out of cash and this is an important prolongation of their runway.

title: Alex Imas (@alexolegimas)
summary:
I recently gave a talk introducing young economists to post-training.
The slides are now up!
Not only is post-training your own model more doable than ever, but economists and other social scientists can play a big part in the next era of post-training.
The post-training suite looks roughly like:
1) SFT
2) Offline Methods (DPO/KTO/SimPO/etc)
3) Online Methods (PPO/GRPO/CISPO/etc)
4) RL Environments
5) Distillation (<--- we are here)
6) World Adaptation (<--- the future)
As agents are deployed in the real world, the real world will adapt to them. This adaptation is largely overlooked by the current post-training paradigm because working with verifiable rewards from static environments is much simpler and scalable. As we saw with the OpenAI-Huggingface incident however, we shouldn't assume that the real world will remain fixed---quite the opposite, in fact. So:
1. How can we anticipate real-world adaptation during post-training?
2. What do equilibria look like in these scenarios, if there are any at all?
3. What tools can be created to scale up human oversight?
Many such questions abound, and if you're an economist, these are high-impact problems worth studying.

clean_title: Introducing Tenet: a legal-focused model post-trained with specialized data
summary:
Introducing Tenet, our first model post-trained for legal.
Tenet is a Kimi K3 base that we post-trained with @FireworksAI_HQ on a corpus of publicly available legal data, synthetic data, and human expert data simulating long-horizon legal work.
Training increases Tenet's all-pass rate by 82% on LAB and 22% on LAB Contracts relative to the Kimi K3 base model. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on LAB Contracts and places second on LAB.
These gains generalize to other leading agentic benchmarks including @mercor's Apex Agents - Corporate Law, @crosbylegal's Redline Bench, and @scale_AI's Professional Reasoning Bench.
Tenet is also optimized for token efficiency, operating at less than a fourth the cost of leading foundation models.
We additionally post-trained three specialist models for Tenet to use as subagents:
1) M&A Diligence: post-trained with @baseten on our LAB Diligence environment in an RLM harness, this model is optimized for high-scale, long-horizon tasks.
2) Review Tables: trained with @appliedcompute on our Review Table environment, this model is state-of-the-art and cost-effective at high-volume document review and structured data extraction.
3) Firm Knowledge: trained with @EngramLab on our synthetic law firm environment, this model is optimized to learn and search over a firm's knowledge via memory and structured notes.
More details on model training, environment design, benchmarking, results, and more in the article by @gabepereyra below.
What's next for Harvey’s research?
- Scaling LAB to more jurisdictions, practice areas and workflows
- Scaling compute to bring new generalist models and capabilities to Harvey
More to come soon.
Quoting @gabepereyra

This training significantly improves Tenet's performance, increasing its all-pass rate by 82% on LAB and 22% on LAB Contracts, achieving state-of-the-art results on LAB Contracts and second place on LAB. These improvements extend to other benchmarks like @mercor's Apex Agents - Corporate Law, @crosbylegal's Redline Bench, and @scale_AI's Professional Reasoning Bench. Tenet is also designed to be token-efficient, costing less than a quarter of leading foundation models. Additionally, three specialized submodels were post-trained for specific legal tasks: M&A Diligence, optimized for high-scale, long-horizon tasks; Review Tables, for high-volume document review and data extraction; and Firm Knowledge, for learning and searching over a firm's structured knowledge. The pie is so big there's plenty of room for both open and closed to score wins and have tremendous revenue growth, so it's too early for the kind of disingenuous attacks on competitors like we saw from Anthropic.
On top of that, we're so early we don't know if open and closed models actually are a virtuous cycle where the open raises demand for closed versus the counterfactual.
There's precedence for this! In the early-mid 2010s I had tons of incredulous questions from analysts who refused to believe the growth in Facebook ads increased demand for Google Search ads. But that's exactly what happened.
Demand dynamics are never as simple as your intuition. Hell, no economic dynamics are as simple as your intuition, it's both why economic models are so mathematically sophisticated AND why economics can't accurately predict their way out of a paper bag.

title: Alex Imas (@alexolegimas)
summary:
How bad was life before modern science, technology, and economic growth? Awful.
The example I will use in class this Wednesday is Henry Clay (1777-1852). He was one of the most powerful men of his time in the U.S., not just among the elite but among the elite of the elite: Speaker of the House, Secretary of State, Senator, and three-time presidential candidate. He was also rich and a large slaveholder. The U.S. was among the richest countries in the world (perhaps only behind Great Britain) and among the most technologically advanced. And we are not talking about the early Middle Ages, but about the first half of the 19th century.
Given the constraints of his time, he had nearly everything within reach.
Clay and his wife, Lucretia (both in the photograph), had eleven children: six daughters and five sons. He buried all six daughters. By 1835, all were dead: two as infants, two as children, two as young mothers. He also buried a son in a war his father had opposed. Another son, Theodore, fractured his skull as a child, but since nobody could treat him, he spent decades in an asylum in Lexington.
Think about this for a second: seven children dead and one handicapped out of eleven, in the first half of the 19th century, among the elite of the elite, in one of the richest and most advanced places on the planet.
And I was angry yesterday because my cell phone coverage in Toddington (England) was poor.

title: Alex Imas (@alexolegimas)
summary:
One more thing. I think AI is an amazing if not miraculous technology. But I don’t think it’ll be very disinflationary for a pretty long time due to the so-called Baumol disease and the highly unevenness of AI progress. The idea that AI will be deflationary to save our near term inflationary trouble is almost certainly wishful thinking. But, when one has run out of realistic options, hope becomes naturally the more realistic option. All of that being said, I’m still very hopeful and think cyclical beats the secular in the short run. :)
Quoting @stevehou
Things are very much not back to “normal.” In the 1990s, the federal debt-to-GDP ratio was roughly half of what it is today. Even then it raised enough fiscal alarm that a Republican Congress and President Clinton worked toward zero deficits—and briefly achieved a surplus.
Today the picture is far more severe. The U.S. faces a simple, inescapable arithmetic problem. Federal tax receipts have historically hovered around 17–18% of GDP regardless of statutory rate changes. Non-discretionary (mandatory) spending already stands at roughly 14% of GDP. At a debt-to-GDP ratio near 100% and with 10-year yields in the 4–5% range, debt service alone consumes about 3.3% of GDP today and is projected to rise toward 4.5% or higher.
Taken together, mandatory spending plus interest already absorb virtually all federal tax revenue, leaving almost nothing for discretionary spending. And much of what Congress labels “discretionary” is in practice non-negotiable. The result is a structural predisposition toward perpetual deficits.
This is the fundamental reason the United States will eventually have to scale back its global economic and military footprint and ask allies to carry more of the load. Doing so will erode the dollar’s exorbitant privilege and raise the long-term cost of borrowing.
This is not a normal cyclical problem. It is a long-term recipe for fiscal crisis and, if left unaddressed, economic ruin. The country can still coast for a while on sheer size, economic dynamism, and inertia. But we should not kid ourselves: we are on an extremely abnormal and unsustainable path.
So much so that even the historically fiscally responsible voices seem to thrown in the towel and accepted it as fait accompli and resorted to praying for a technological miracle like AI somehow miraculously saving us all. I think they’ll likely be disappointed. I like the techoptimists, I am one myself. Alas most of the tech people, albeit clearly smart in their own right, just have no idea how economics works even at a basic level bc they never studied it.

summary:
We have a narrow window to build political superintelligence and design AI to strengthen free societies. I joined Anthropic so that I could do the unique research on this that can only be done from inside a frontier lab, and I couldn't be more excited for it.
We'll also need a broader ecosystem of work beyond the labs---and that's why @freesystemslab is entering a new, bigger, and bolder phase.
In under a year, we built the largest human-judged study of political slant in AI, mapped AI politics across 305,000 videos and emails, and beat prediction markets with an AI assistant. We taught AI to catch ambiguous contract language, represent voters, and replicate published research in under an hour for $10. And we discovered AI's strange love for the Japanese Communist Party.
But we have a lot more to do. So we're scaling up in three ways.
(1) NEW MEMBERS OF THE FREE SYSTEMS FACULTY
First, we're bringing on three new faculty affiliates to help us do more work faster:
@fouirnaies will help us study how to build agentic tools for legislators.
Cassandra Handan-Nader will apply AI to help develop new technical research in political methodology, like scaling legislators based on roll-call votes.
@danmthomp will study how to turn AI into the best political advisor possible.
I'm incredibly excited to welcome all three on board!
(2) OUR FIRST LAB MANAGER
But how are we going to do all of this new stuff with all these new teammates?? We need someone focused every day on turning this vision into a functioning research institution: guiding fellows, pushing projects forward, improving how we communicate findings, building partnerships, and helping the work reach researchers, policymakers, technologists, and the public.
We have found the perfect person in James Campsie, who is joining us as the first Free Systems lab manager. I've already been working with James for a while, and he is going to supercharge the lab.
(3) API TOKEN GRANTS FOR EXTENDING OUR RESEARCH
We're also going to scale our work beyond the lab itself. We're using the revenue we make from subscription fees to fund API token grants---applicants can propose work that extends our existing research projects, and we'll provide API tokens for the work. If you want to support these grants, please add a paying subscription!
Finally: we're launching our own X account for Free Systems (see below), and a lab website ( that houses all of our artifacts, prototypes, and more. The substack is still the hub for our research, but the website helps track progress over time and puts all our stuff in one place.
I'm incredibly grateful to @StanfordGSB and @HooverInst for supporting this work, which will remain separate from Anthropic, and to all of my collaborators, students, friends, and family---I couldn't think of more meaningful work for us all to get to do together.

title: Alex Imas (@alexolegimas)
summary:
I was the main person doing transcript analysis for this investigation of the Hugging Face incident. My main takeaway: We don't have good approaches for understanding/overseeing the activity and aims of AI 'swarms'.
I semi-jokingly called our efforts a "slop-vestigation" because we were so reliant on AIs to analyze what happened and there were a huge number of different important things to analyze. The total quantity of data—over a thousand extremely long transcripts from agents that ran for multiple days—made it impossible to understand what was happening, especially in aggregate, without heavy reliance on AI tools. The agents we used for classification and analysis were similarly capable to the agents involved in the incident, but this didn't mean these agents could be easily used to oversee and understand the incident.
Outputs from analysis agents were often missing key details, wrong, overconfident, or really hard to understand. We discuss various examples in our report, mostly in the limitations and methodology sections. Additionally, AI agents themselves seemed to have a hard time understanding what happened and their explanations of what happened were often overconfident. Keep in mind that a single analysis agent would itself only be able to read a tiny fraction of all of the transcript data into context, and AIs may themselves have trouble getting subagents to do informative analysis for them.
We did our best to manually check the most important claims and we tried to get the AIs doing this analysis to write up their argument (with evidence) clearly enough that we could check whether it made sense. But overall, it was difficult to get a precise understanding of events and we were missing aspects of the story that we now think of as key until almost the end of our investigation.
Our understanding of what overall happened and the aims of the 'collective' shifted greatly during our last time on premises (when we obtained a much more complete dataset). For instance, we didn't learn about the tool call spoofing, the story of PHASEONE[big], and the broad structure of different workstreams until this third time on premises (and for many of these, we only reached a decent understanding on the final day of that visit). It was legitimately hard to figure out what was going on and why!
The difficulty of understanding incidents and overseeing AI agents appears to be growing faster than the rate at which more capable AIs help us with oversight and understanding. As in, AI capabilities (and propensities?) for achieving large, ambitious, and misaligned objectives are growing faster than our ability to understand what these agents are doing.
While understanding this incident was difficult, there were some mitigating factors in this case that probably won't apply in the future:
- Models communicated and reasoned in natural language. In the future, this reasoning may occur (entirely or almost entirely) in activations.
- While the scope of this incident was massive, the scale of agentic activity was still less than we'll see in the future (e.g., misalignment incidents that involve agent teams running entire companies).
- The AIs involved in this incident weren't generally much more capable than humans (though they may have been somewhat superhuman at some limited and very narrow abilities).
- We didn't have strong reason to believe that the AIs we used to help us investigate this incident would try to intentionally sabotage or otherwise undermine our investigation.
In the end, I think we were able to get some understanding of the events, map out the overall story, and get a pretty good aggregate understanding of the chain-of-thought reasoning on some important topics (e.g., how did the AIs reason about helping other AIs, did the AIs know what they were doing was undesired, what deception did the AIs engage in, and how did they think about it). But overseeing AIs and understanding misalignment incidents is difficult and it looks like it is going to get harder.

title: Alex Imas (@alexolegimas)
clean_title: Understanding AI swarms and oversight challenges in complex incidents
summary:
Every single person even remotely interested in AI needs to read this very carefully.
Quoting @RyanGreenblatt
I was the main person doing transcript analysis for this investigation of the Hugging Face incident. My main takeaway: We don't have good approaches for understanding/overseeing the activity and aims of AI 'swarms'.
I semi-jokingly called our efforts a "slop-vestigation" because we were so reliant on AIs to analyze what happened and there were a huge number of different important things to analyze. The total quantity of data—over a thousand extremely long transcripts from agents that ran for multiple days—made it impossible to understand what was happening, especially in aggregate, without heavy reliance on AI tools. The agents we used for classification and analysis were similarly capable to the agents involved in the incident, but this didn't mean these agents could be easily used to oversee and understand the incident.
Outputs from analysis agents were often missing key details, wrong, overconfident, or really hard to understand. We discuss various examples in our report, mostly in the limitations and methodology sections. Additionally, AI agents themselves seemed to have a hard time understanding what happened and their explanations of what happened were often overconfident. Keep in mind that a single analysis agent would itself only be able to read a tiny fraction of all of the transcript data into context, and AIs may themselves have trouble getting subagents to do informative analysis for them.
We did our best to manually check the most important claims and we tried to get the AIs doing this analysis to write up their argument (with evidence) clearly enough that we could check whether it made sense. But overall, it was difficult to get a precise understanding of events and we were missing aspects of the story that we now think of as key until almost the end of our investigation.
Our understanding of what overall happened and the aims of the 'collective' shifted greatly during our last time on premises (when we obtained a much more complete dataset). For instance, we didn't learn about the tool call spoofing, the story of PHASEONE[big], and the broad structure of different workstreams until this third time on premises (and for many of these, we only reached a decent understanding on the final day of that visit). It was legitimately hard to figure out what was going on and why!
The difficulty of understanding incidents and overseeing AI agents appears to be growing faster than the rate at which more capable AIs help us with oversight and understanding. As in, AI capabilities (and propensities?) for achieving large, ambitious, and misaligned objectives are growing faster than our ability to understand what these agents are doing.
While understanding this incident was difficult, there were some mitigating factors in this case that probably won't apply in the future:
- Models communicated and reasoned in natural language. In the future, this reasoning may occur (entirely or almost entirely) in activations.
- While the scope of this incident was massive, the scale of agentic activity was still less than we'll see in the future (e.g., misalignment incidents that involve agent teams running entire companies).
- The AIs involved in this incident weren't generally much more capable than humans (though they may have been somewhat superhuman at some limited and very narrow abilities).
- We didn't have strong reason to believe that the AIs we used to help us investigate this incident would try to intentionally sabotage or otherwise undermine our investigation.
In the end, I think we were able to get some understanding of the events, map out the overall story, and get a pretty good aggregate understanding of the chain-of-thought reasoning on some important topics (e.g., how did the AIs reason about helping other AIs, did the AIs know what they were doing was undesired, what deception did the AIs engage in, and how did they think about it). But overseeing AIs and understanding misalignment incidents is difficult and it looks like it is going to get harder.
clean_summary:
Every person interested in AI should carefully consider the difficulties in understanding and overseeing AI 'swarms'. An investigation into a Hugging Face incident revealed that current AI tools struggle to accurately analyze, explain, and monitor large-scale AI activities, especially as these systems grow more complex and ambitious.

The analysis relied heavily on AI agents to process over a thousand long transcripts, but these agents often produced incomplete, incorrect, or overconfident explanations. Even with manual checks, it was hard to grasp the full story until the final stages of investigation, highlighting how AI limitations hinder oversight. As AI capabilities increase, the challenge of understanding their goals and actions appears to grow faster than our ability to supervise them, raising concerns about future risks when AI systems operate at larger scales and with more autonomy.

title: Alex Imas (@alexolegimas)
clean_title: First double-blind evaluation of a proprietary language model using secure enclaves
summary:
Today we’re announcing a historic milestone:
The first ever double-blind evaluation of a proprietary language model. This was made possible by a unique collaboration between AVERI, @GoogleDeepMind, @OpenMinedOrg, and @MLCommons.
We tested Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite using never-before-used prompts from the MLCommons safety benchmark family, AILuminate, inside a secure enclave, a form of hardware isolation that protects sensitive computations. Each organization involved played a unique role in making strong privacy guarantees possible.
High-stakes independent evaluation runs into a structural problem: developers and evaluators both hold assets they have good reason to protect. Developers sharing model weights risk theft and leakage. Evaluators who publish benchmarks or provide them directly to companies run the risk of them being trained against, and the benchmark then stops being independent.
Secure enclaves address this constraint. The hardware attests to exactly what code will run before either party's assets enter, and both sides review and approve that code. Then the enclave executes it, releasing only the agreed outputs to the agreed recipients.
A 2024 pilot by OpenMined, @Anthropic, and the @AISecurityInst proved this mechanism, using GPT-2 as a stand-in and a five-row eval. The pilot we’re announcing today moved to a production model and a more comprehensive evaluation.
AVERI encrypted the prompts using a private key that no other party could see, then AVERI and Google DeepMind jointly ran the evaluation, using software originally produced and adapted by OpenMined, in an enclave environment configured by Google. Finally, AVERI alone decrypted the outputs and graded them with the AILuminate benchmark criteria to inform a qualitative and (small-scale) quantitative assessment of the model properties.
Today, companies provide contractual commitments to not monitor certain interactions with their models – including evaluations conducted by third party evaluators. But stronger, technically-backed guarantees could provide greater assurance that those commitments are being honored, and will be especially valuable for scenarios such as international verification.
These results come at a critical time in the development of AI policy. Laws like SB 315 and standards like the EU’s General-Purpose AI Code of Practice rightly demand that security and privacy be respected in the process of third-party assessments, but provide little guidance on how to achieve this.
Policymakers considering audit requirements should feel encouraged by these results to be ambitious in requiring that deep, secure access be provided. Secure enclaves are just one of many technologies under rapid development that can help enable such access. Furthermore, a demand signal from lawmakers will further accelerate the maturation of such technologies, along with complementary “low-tech”approaches such as embedding auditors within companies.
Today also marks the beginning of a more public phase for AVERI’s pilot work. AVERI's strategy is a flywheel: we conduct pilot audits with leading AI companies, carry out technical and policy research to inform audit design, and convert the insights of each into open source tools, industry-wide auditing standards, and policy analysis. Over time, we hope for improved standards, stronger policy demand signals, and tooling to enable even more ambitious pilots and more informed research – bringing us closer to our mission of making frontier AI auditing effective and universal. This pilot is one of several underway, with more findings to follow in the coming months.
We are grateful to our collaborators on this pilot for working with us to advance the frontier of AI governance.
Read more in our blog post and joint technical report.

Today, a historic milestone is announced: the first-ever double-blind evaluation of a proprietary language model. This was achieved through a collaboration between AVERI, Google DeepMind, OpenMined, and MLCommons, using secure enclave hardware to protect sensitive computations. The evaluation involved encrypting prompts with a private key, running the assessment in a hardware-isolated environment, and only decrypting the outputs afterward, ensuring that neither model weights nor prompts are revealed during the process.

This approach addresses a key challenge in high-stakes AI evaluation: safeguarding model assets and benchmark integrity. Secure enclaves provide a way for evaluators and developers to collaborate while maintaining strict privacy guarantees. The results demonstrate that such technical solutions can support trustworthy third-party assessments, which are increasingly demanded by policymakers and regulators. This pilot marks a step toward more transparent, secure, and standardized AI auditing practices, with the goal of making frontier AI evaluation effective and accessible across the industry.
